reason: General technique from this episode: a test that scans source or declarations to enforce a rule can pass while blind. Proving it catches a deliberate violation is the cheap check. Class-level, so later guard tests reuse it. Project level because its worked example names this repo's walk.

The same "prove it can fail before trusting green" discipline applies to a behavioural regression test for a fix, and that case currently has no trigger here; the procedure was only in metaform-development.
Behavioural regression proof for a UI fix was done correctly here (copy, revert, fail with the defect's value, pass with fix, delete scratch); recording that as the rule for the class.

A regression check was proven to fail on the reverted copy, but its assertion still passed for the wrong reason (it matched a later seat reply, not the held one). The proof step needs to require the assertion to name the exact output the fix must keep.

The elevenlabs regression check first passed with 1 request instead of 2 because its urlopen stub answered, and the answer was cached. Switching the stub to refuse exposed the second request. The copy-first procedure proved the fix.
The episode traced which path delivered an answer by editing the shared tree with probes and restoring by cp, which the existing shared-tree rule forbids; the probe-in-copy procedure is the lesson.

On 2026-10-14 the F4 agent's regression test passed on the shared tree only because a parallel agent had already landed the F3 fix there. Proof came from a /tmp copy built from HEAD's files plus a one-line hook, which failed on the defect's own assertion. The skill describes the copy but not this case.

A new CLI verb that syncs over the network failed the open-world evidence registry until it had a reasoned entry. The fix was the registry entry, and the walk stayed as it was. That is a repeatable pitfall for any module verb.

Ticket 574e48c5 (#16): a first mutant failed with AttributeError ('Project' object has no attribute 'id') before reaching the assertion, so it proved nothing until corrected. The 'nothing in home A' check looked at home/projects/proj/source_placement, a path the code no longer used, so it could never fail; a second mutant that writes into home A was needed to show it has teeth. The original _move_runs file was never committed, so a behaviour-reproducing mutant was the only proof available.

A race fix was judged by one green run; the trace showed narrow race windows only reproduce at a given worker count and in a fraction of runs, so the before/after proof needs repetition and enough concurrency.

The HEAD-copy "before" run first failed on a missing fixture file under the copy's tests/fixtures, not on the defect's assertion; copying the fixtures folder was needed before the real assertion failure appeared.
